action: Never send crypto to an address shown in a livestream or QR code, however famous the presenter; no genuine service doubles what you send. Staff who handle crypto should be reminded of this giveaway scam pattern.
date_note: Date is Coinbase's blog post (Tuesday, November 17); The Block says the livestream ran earlier, 'last month', and Coinbase did not say when.
exec: Deepfake giveaway scams are drawing real customer money; a large exchange says its AI stopped most of the transfers, but the rest reached the scammers.
geo_basis: company HQ (Coinbase is remote-first; US country centroid used)
plain: Scammers streamed a fake Tesla event on YouTube with a deepfake of Elon Musk promising to double any crypto sent. Coinbase says its AI stopped about $4.7 million of customer transfers to the scammers.
summary: Coinbase says scammers ran a YouTube livestream imitating a Tesla 'flying car' demo, with a deepfake of Elon Musk, wallet addresses and a QR code promising to double any crypto sent. Over about two hours hundreds of its customers tried to send funds; Coinbase says its AI blocked about $4.7 million, roughly 91% of attempts. It says no accounts were hacked.
title: Coinbase says AI blocked $4.7 million of transfers to deepfake Elon Musk crypto giveaway scam

validation.note: The Block and Bitcoin Magazine both report Coinbase's own blog post (not opened: it returned 403; BleepingComputer also 403). The 91% and $4.7 million figures are Coinbase's; the amount that reached scammers was not stated.

key_findings: About $4.7 million blocked, about 91% of attempted transfers.
More than 500,000 viewers of the fake stream, per Coinbase.
Coinbase says nobody was hacked; customers approved the sends themselves.
recommendations: Do not send crypto to addresses shown in livestreams.
